title: Adaptive Utensil & Hand-Grip System
summary: A family of 3D-printed, user-fitted grips that help people with limited hand function hold utensils, pens and everyday tools.
context: University internship — Occupational Therapy Partner Program

cover.alt: Flat lay of teal and white 3D-printed adaptive grips with calipers and sketches

problem: Off-the-shelf foam grips wear out quickly and rarely fit hands affected by arthritis, cerebral palsy or spinal cord injury, forcing therapists to improvise with tape and putty.
requirements: Fit a range of hand sizes and grip patterns from a single parametric model
Be dishwasher-safe and printable in under two hours
Accept standard cutlery handles from 8 to 14 mm wide
Allow a therapist to adjust fit without CAD experience
approach: I built a parametric Fusion 360 model driven by five hand measurements, so a therapist enters values and exports a printable file. Soft TPU zones were added where users reported pressure points.

humanStory.abstract: When an everyday grip does not fit, a simple task like holding a utensil or pen can take extra effort and make existing aids hard to use.
humanStory.detail: Therapists often have to adapt off-the-shelf grips by hand, but each person holds tools differently. The project makes that fitting process more personal: a small set of measurements shapes a grip around the user's hand and the task they want to do.

processFlow.title: Observation
processFlow.body: Shadowed therapy sessions to record grip types and failure points of existing aids.

processFlow.title: Parametric modelling
processFlow.body: Created a configurable model with user-parameter tables for diameter, angle and strap position.

processFlow.title: Rapid iteration
processFlow.body: Printed and tested 11 iterations with six users, refining wall thickness and strap geometry.

processFlow.title: Does the grip fit the task?
Fabrication
processFlow.body: Printed on FDM machines in PLA for rigid cores and TPU 95A for contact surfaces, using a two-material print with a mechanical interlock instead of adhesive.

outcome: The therapy team now prints personalised grips in-house. Average fitting time dropped from a full session to under 20 minutes.

gallery.caption: Prototype family, iterations 4–9
gallery.backText: Eleven printed iterations were tested with six users to tune fit, wall thickness and strap geometry.

gallery.backText: Five hand measurements drive the configurable model so a therapist can prepare a personalized file.
